data.content_ref: inline:The target explicitly disclaims any forward-looking probabilistic commitment, stating the preference 'makes no claim about the future probability of the theory being true; it only asserts that, relative to our current critical discussion, this theory is the most worthy of further testing.' Yet within the same claim it also characterizes the surviving theory as 'the best available target for future criticism.' The phrase 'best available target for future criticism' is itself a comparative, forward-looking optimality judgment: it ranks theories by their expected fruitfulness for an activity (criticism) that has not yet occurred. One cannot coherently assert 'this theory is the best target for future criticism' while simultaneously insisting the preference entails no expectation about the future. A purely synchronic, non-inductive statement would be 'this theory has, to date, survived the severest tests' — a description of the past. Calling it the best target for future criticism converts that retrospective description into a prospective recommendation, which is precisely the inductive move (past survival ⇒ future promise) the target purports to exclude. Thus the target's own wording contradicts its central disclaimer: it smuggles a forward-looking expectation into what it presents as a merely procedural, present-tense rule. This is a distinct internal inconsistency from the prior objection (which targeted the loss of verisimilitude and practical prediction); here the contradiction is within the target's own articulation of what the preference does and does not assert.
